collections.title: Bone and muscle
collections.intro: Without gravity, bones lose mineral and muscles shrink. Watch how crews fight back with about two hours of exercise a day.

items.title: Fincke exercises on the RED in the Node 1 module during Expedition 9
items.caption: The interim resistive exercise device (IRED) gave early station crews a way to load their legs and spine with squats and lifts.

items.title: Culbertson exercises on TVIS in the Service Module during Expedition Three
items.caption: Running on the TVIS treadmill, held down by a harness. Impact loading helps protect bone density in the legs and hips.

items.title: Flight Engineer Donald R. Pettit exercises on the TVIS in the SM during Expedition Six
items.caption: Treadmill runs are a daily countermeasure: they keep the heart, legs and bones working against a pull that is no longer there.

items.title: Swanson exercises on COLBERT in Node 3
items.caption: COLBERT, the station treadmill. Crews log many kilometres on it to preserve fitness and bone.

items.title: Burbank exercises on the ARED in the Node 3
items.caption: The ARED lifts real loads without gravity, using vacuum cylinders. It is the main defence against bone and muscle loss on station.

items.title: Kuipers exercises on the ARED
items.caption: Squats and deadlifts on the ARED load the hips and spine, the bones that lose the most in orbit.

items.title: ISS Expedition 18 Sandra Magnus uses Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED)
items.caption: Resistance exercise has to be done with the body strapped in so the force goes into the bones, not the room.

items.title: Hadfield exercises on the ARED in the Node 3
items.caption: Strength training on the ARED. Exercise time is scheduled into every crew day like any other task.

items.title: CCP Astronauts - CMS Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED) O
items.caption: Crews practise on the ground before flight so the routine is familiar when it counts.

items.title: MARES
items.caption: MARES measures how strongly astronauts' joints and muscles can work, to see how spaceflight changes them.

items.title: How Do Astronauts Exercise in Space?
items.caption: A plain-language tour of the running, cycling and lifting that keeps crews healthy.

items.title: ARED physical training with Mike Hopkins
items.caption: A commercial crew astronaut trains on the same resistive device the station uses.

collections.title: Radiation
collections.intro: Beyond Earth's magnetic shield, radiation is the hazard with no easy fix. These are the instruments and dummies that measure it.

items.title: Pesquet conducts ESA-Active-Dosimeters Experiment OPS in Columbus
items.caption: An astronaut works with active dosimeters, small instruments that log the radiation dose a crew receives.

items.title: Hadfield holds bubble detectors for the RaDI-N Experiment in the Columbus Module
items.caption: Bubble detectors grow tiny bubbles when neutrons hit them, a simple way to count radiation dose.

items.title: Active Tissue Equivalent Dosimeter
items.caption: A tissue-equivalent dosimeter, built to read dose the way human tissue would absorb it.

items.title: ISS HERA
items.caption: HERA, a monitor that tracks radiation levels around the station in real time.

items.title: Matroshka-R Phantom experiment
items.caption: The Matroshka phantom is a human-shaped model packed with detectors, showing how deep radiation reaches inside a body.

items.title: Matroshka-2 Kibo Hardware
items.caption: A Matroshka phantom set up in the Kibo module, measuring dose at the organs.

items.title: MATRYOSHKA-R (RBO-3-2) Radiation Suite in the Service Module (SM)
items.caption: Radiation detectors in the Service Module, part of a long-running dose-mapping effort.

items.title: iss061e145988
items.caption: The AstroRad vest is designed to shield blood-forming organs during a solar particle event.

items.title: Phantom torso in the Human Research Facility
items.caption: A torso model with dosimeters inside, used to measure how much radiation reaches the organs.

items.title: How NASA Will Protect Astronauts From Space Radiation
items.caption: How NASA plans to protect astronauts from solar and cosmic radiation on longer trips.

items.caption: A radiation instrument that measures how hard each particle hits, which sets biological risk.

collections.title: Sleep and isolation
collections.intro: Sixteen sunrises a day, small cabins and months away from home. Sleep and mood need as much care as muscle.

items.title: Coleman in sleeping quarters
items.caption: A station sleeping quarters. Each crew member gets a small private booth with a sleeping bag tied to the wall.

items.title: Expedition 26 Crewmembers in sleeping quarters
items.caption: Three crew members peek out of their sleeping quarters on Christmas morning. Sleep stays on a fixed schedule even though the sun rises every 90 minutes.

items.title: View inside the crew quarters
items.caption: The inside of a crew quarters booth: the quiet, dark place an astronaut uses to sleep.

items.title: Cristoforetti in Crew quarters
items.caption: An astronaut in her sleeping bag in her personal crew quarters. A private space helps with sleep and mood on long missions.

items.title: Skylab astronaut strapped into a sleep restraint
items.caption: On Skylab in 1973, sleep restraints stopped crew drifting off while they slept.

items.title: Whitson in her TeSS in the Destiny U.S. Lab during STS-111 UF-2 docked OPS
items.caption: Peggy Whitson at the temporary sleep station set up in the US lab in 2002, before permanent crew quarters.

items.title: How Do Astronauts Practice Self-Care in Space?
items.caption: Music, movies and rest: how crews recharge when home is 250 miles below.

items.title: How Will Deep Space Travel Affect Artemis Astronauts’ Health and Performance?
items.caption: Wristbands record sleep and movement on Artemis II to show how crews adjust to a small cabin.

items.title: HERA crew answers students
items.caption: A crew living in an Earth-based isolation habitat tells students what the confinement is like.

items.title: 10 Days in Orion
items.caption: How four astronauts will live, eat and sleep in the Orion capsule on a Moon trip.

items.title: CHAPEA 2, audio log 1 (podcast)
items.caption: The commander describes the first night in the Mars habitat.

items.title: CHAPEA 2, audio log 2 (podcast)
items.caption: What a typical day looks like for a crew shut in for a year.

items.title: CHAPEA 2, audio log 3 (podcast)
items.caption: The crew talks about sleep patterns, activity and interaction, the things NASA is tracking.

items.title: ISS results: wayfinding (podcast)
items.caption: Researchers discuss how sleep, isolation and confinement affect astronauts on top of weightlessness.

collections.title: Twins Study
collections.intro: Scott Kelly spent a year in orbit while his identical twin Mark stayed on Earth. Their differences show what space does to a body.

items.title: Kelly during Twins Study Experiment Operations
items.caption: Scott Kelly gives himself a flu shot for the immune-system part of the Twins Study. Mark got the same study on Earth.

items.title: Expedition 43 Kelly Brothers
items.caption: Scott and Mark Kelly before launch. Having an identical twin on the ground made this a one-of-a-kind comparison.

items.title: Expedition 43 Kelly Brothers
items.caption: The twins pose together at Baikonur before Scott launches on his one-year mission.

items.title: Expedition 43 Press Conference
items.caption: Mark Kelly fist-bumps his twin through the glass before launch.

items.title: Mark and Scott Kelly talk to news media
items.caption: The brothers speak with reporters about the mission. Researchers followed both for blood, genes, gut bacteria and more.

items.title: Expedition 25 Docking
items.caption: Mark Kelly speaks to his twin by phone while Scott was aboard the station in 2010.

items.title: jsc2011e026383
items.caption: The twins reunited after an earlier flight. Both are astronauts, which made them closely matched test subjects.

items.title: Kelly in Node 1
items.caption: Scott Kelly in the station's Node 1, partway through his year in space.

items.caption: Scott Kelly, who spent 340 days in space, gives advice on readjusting to life on Earth.

collections.title: Life support / CO₂
collections.intro: Every breath adds CO₂ to a sealed cabin. Scrubbers, oxygen makers and water recyclers keep the air safe.

items.title: Sabatier
items.caption: Installing the Sabatier system, which turns CO₂ and hydrogen into water and methane so the station recovers more water.

items.title: Node-3 CDRA (Carbon Dioxide Removal Assembly) R&R
items.caption: Replacing parts of the CO₂ removal assembly (CDRA) in Node 3. It scrubs carbon dioxide from cabin air.

items.title: Node 3 CDRA Replacement
items.caption: Scott Kelly and Terry Virts replace a CDRA part, routine upkeep that keeps CO₂ low.

items.title: Marshburn performs maintenance on the CDRA in the JPM
items.caption: Maintenance on the CDRA in the Japanese module. Crews fix their own air system in orbit.

items.title: iss071e549503
items.caption: An astronaut removes a carbon dioxide system part during a repair.

items.title: Hydrogen Sensor Oxygen Generation System (OGS) Remove and Replace (R&R)
items.caption: Hydrogen sensor work on the oxygen generator, which splits water to make breathable air.

items.title: OGA Hydrogen ORU R&R - NOD3A5 Part 5
items.caption: Swapping a part of the oxygen generation assembly, the machine that makes the station's air.

items.title: ISS Expedition 18 Water Recovery System (WRS) Leak Check
items.caption: Checking the water recovery system for leaks. It turns sweat and urine back into drinking water.

items.title: Water recovery and management on the ISS (diagram)
items.caption: A diagram of how water flows through the station's recycling loop.

items.title: Dava Newman tours the ECLSS lab
items.caption: NASA's life support lab at Marshall, where the next generation of air and water hardware is tested.

items.title: NASA ScienceCasts: ECLSS on Station
items.caption: How the station's life support system keeps the air breathable and the water clean.

items.title: NASA ScienceCasts: Water Recovery on the Space Station
items.caption: The station now recycles 98% of the water its crew uses.

collections.title: Spacewalks
collections.intro: A spacewalk means hours in a pressurised suit, a long day for the heart, hands and nerves. Here is how crews prepare.

items.title: EMU 3003 and 3005 OFV
items.caption: Suit hardware being prepared. The spacesuit is a personal spacecraft that supplies oxygen and keeps pressure steady.

items.title: Mastracchio during EVA 2
items.caption: An astronaut outside the station on a spacewalk. Hours of suit work tire the hands and shoulders.

items.title: Whitson during EVA 13
items.caption: Peggy Whitson on a spacewalk. Suits are pressurised, so even gripping a tool takes effort.

items.title: Spacewalk 23 view
items.caption: A view from a spacewalk where a crew member works at the end of a long day outside.

items.title: View during 2nd EVA on ISS stack
items.caption: A view during the second spacewalk on the early station stack, 1998.

items.title: Tanner performs first EVA during STS-115 / Expedition 13 joint operations
items.caption: A shuttle-era spacewalk during the building of the station.

items.title: MS Wolf prepares for EVA 2
items.caption: An astronaut gets ready for a spacewalk. Preparing the suit and body is half the job.

items.title: STS-64 Extravehicular activity (EVA) training view in WETF
items.caption: Training for spacewalks in the pool, which mimics weightlessness for suited astronauts.

items.title: Spacewalk 101
items.caption: A NASA flight director explains how spacewalks work and what crews go through.

items.title: Suiting Up for a Spacewalk
items.caption: The long process of getting into a suit before stepping outside.

items.caption: Volunteers live in a pressure chamber to test how the body responds to the pressure changes of a spacewalk.
